# Timeline of the introduction of color television in countries and territories
## List in alphabetical order by country and territory
| Argentina * | 1978/1980 | LS 82 Canal 7 | PAL | Introduced for the 1978 FIFA World Cup by A78TV (Argentina 78 TV), a purpose-built system that took over the signals of channels 7 and 13 for the telecast of the Cup's games, even though only the finals and several second-round matches were broadcast in color for the domestic market. LS 82 Canal 7 became ATC (Argentina Televisora Color) on 3 May 1979, with partial color telecasts, which were officially authorized to begin, at is full, at midnight on Thursday, 1 May 1980 on both ATC and LS 85 Canal 13, the latter of which had carried out late-night tests for several months beforehand and previously undertook non-public experimental transmissions under the NTSC system in 1969, but the project was cancelled due to lack of government approval but they returned in 1971 with non satisfactory results. Full-time color transmissions by late 1980-early 1981. Color broadcasts had been available from Brazil since 1972, Chile and Paraguay since 1978. Uses the PAL-N system. |  
| Armenia *. - Armenian SSR | 1973/1981 | Armenia 1 | SECAM, PAL | First transmission was the 1973 [May Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Workers'_Day "International Workers' Day")Parade in Yerevan. Full-time color transmissions since 1981.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_introduction_of_color_television_in_countries_and_territories#cite_note-2) |  
| Aruba | 1973/1977 | Telearuba | NTSC | Color broadcasting was introduced in 1973 after tests, but there were still black and white programs that were received from Venezuela until around 1977.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_introduction_of_color_television_in_countries_and_territories#cite_note-3) |  

# Timeline of the introduction of color television in countries and territories
## List in alphabetical order by country and territory
| Australia * | 1967/1971/1974/1975 | ATV-0 (now ATV-10). | PAL | Permanent color telecasts since Saturday, 1 March 1975. First color test broadcast on Thursday, 15 June 1967, with live coverage of the Pakenham races.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_introduction_of_color_television_in_countries_and_territories#cite_note-4) Many television shows were produced and broadcast in color between 1972 and 1974, with limited color telecasts from mid-1974 on. |  
| Austria * | 1969/1975 | ORF | PAL | First transmission was the Eurovision broadcast of the New Year Concert from Vienna on Wednesday, 1 January 1969. Full-time color transmissions since 15 January 1975. |  
| Azerbaijan *. - Azerbaijan SSR | 1973/1978 | AzTV | SECAM, PAL | First color broadcasts in Azerbaijan started in 1973 using the SECAM standard. Full color service started in 1978. |  
| Bahamas * | 1983 | ZNS-TV | NTSC | Color transmissions had been available from Miami since 1954 (WTVJ) and West Palm Beach since the late 1950s[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_introduction_of_color_television_in_countries_and_territories#cite_note-5) |  

# Timeline of the introduction of color television in countries and territories
## List in alphabetical order by country and territory
| Bangladesh * | 1980 | BTV | PAL | Color transmissions launched by President Ziaur Rahman on 16 December 1980, marking the first official full-time color broadcasts in South Asia.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_introduction_of_color_television_in_countries_and_territories#cite_note-eknojor-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_introduction_of_color_television_in_countries_and_territories#cite_note-agrajatra-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_introduction_of_color_television_in_countries_and_territories#cite_note-power-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_introduction_of_color_television_in_countries_and_territories#cite_note-9) |  
| Barbados * | 1971/1984 | CBC | NTSC |  |  
| Belarus *. - Byelorussian SSR | 1974 | Belteleradio | SECAM | Full-time color service came in 1974[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_introduction_of_color_television_in_countries_and_territories#cite_note-10) with SECAM. |  
| Belize | 1984 | Channel 7 | NTSC | Color broadcasts have been available from Mexico since 1964. |  
| Benin | 1982 | OTRB | SECAM |  |  
| Belgium * | 1971/1977 | RTB BRT | PAL | Color broadcasts from France (SECAM), Germany and The Netherlands (PAL) were available since 1967. Early receivers were very costly owing to multiple standards: PAL/SECAM/625 lines and monochrome/819 lines. |  
| Bermuda * | 1968/1970/1971_[citation needed_] | ZBM-TV ZFB-TV | NTSC |  |  

# Timeline of the introduction of color television in countries and territories
## List in alphabetical order by country and territory
| Bolivia * | 1976/1980 | TV Boliviana | NTSC | Experimental color broadcasts began in 1976; the first station to broadcast in color was Televisión Universitaria UAJMS from Tarija.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_introduction_of_color_television_in_countries_and_territories#cite_note-TVU-11) Full-time color arrived in 1980. Color broadcasts have been available from Brazil since 1972, but were PAL-M. |  
| Bosnia and Herzegovina *. - SR Bosnia and Herzegovina | 1972/1975_[citation needed_] | Radiotelevizija Sarajevo (now BHT1). | PAL | First color transmission came from Belgrade in December 1971,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_introduction_of_color_television_in_countries_and_territories#cite_note-rtvslon.ba-12) local service began regular color broadcasts in 1972,_[citation needed_] but some programmes on Televizija Sarajevo began broadcasting in color by 1974,_[citation needed_] and full-time broadcasts began in early/mid 1975 when news programs, such as Dnevnik started to broadcast its editions in color._[citation needed_] |  

# Timeline of the introduction of color television in countries and territories
## List in alphabetical order by country and territory
| Russia *. - Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic | 1967/1973/1977 | Soviet Central Television (now Channel One). | OSKM, SECAM | Test color broadcasting started in Moscow as early as 14 January 1960 using the OSKM system (based on NTSC, which was adapted to the European 625 lines standard, using a 4.43 MHz color subcarrier) from the Moscow Experimental TV Studio at Shabolovka street, but lasted only a few months as this system was rejected. Only about 4000 television sets were built for this system (Raduga, Temp 22, Izumrud 201/203). SECAM broadcasting was introduced specifically for the 50th Golden Jubilee Anniversary of the October Revolution in 1967. The Song of the Year festival and the New Year's address by the leader of the USSR began to be filmed in color in 1973. Full-time colorcasts began between 1977 and 1978, but however, there were small stations at the edge of the country in places such as Siberia finishing the switch in 1987.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_introduction_of_color_television_in_countries_and_territories#cite_note-110)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_introduction_of_color_television_in_countries_and_territories#cite_note-111) Some parts of the USSR received color from Alaska since 1966 in some circumstances when signals were not jammed in some parts and were received by contraband receivers to pick up signals._[citation needed_] |  
| Saint Kitts and Nevis. - Saint Christopher, Nevis and Anguilla | 1981 | ZIZ-TV | NTSC | This former British colony is the current Saint Kitts and Nevis. Color broadcasts have been available from Guadeloupe since 1972, but were SECAM. Full-color broadcast since 1981. |  

# Timeline of the introduction of color television in countries and territories
## List in alphabetical order by country and territory
| Saint Pierre and Miquelon * | 1967 | RFO (1ère SPM TV; Previously known as ORTF) | SECAM | Color transmissions had been available from Newfoundland and Labrador since 1967, but were NTSC. There are transmitters in SPM that can carry a signal from Newfoundland and Labrador which converts it to SECAM from NTSC and in some cases, In Fortune, Newfoundland, 1ère is converted to NTSC by a transmitter that is placed there. |  
| Saudi Arabia * | 1973 | SAGTS | SECAM |  |  
| Senegal * | 1975 | RTS | SECAM |  |  
| Serbia *. - SR Serbia | 1971/1979 | Televizija Beograd (now RTS1). | PAL | Introduced on the launch of the second TVB channel (TVB 2) on New Year's Eve of 1971,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_introduction_of_color_television_in_countries_and_territories#cite_note-rtvslon.ba-12) as it was the first Yugoslav channel to start in color. From the late 1970s, TVB 1 switched to color, thus making all channels broadcast in color. (both TVB 1 and TVB 2, as they were only the channels available in that time) Full-time color broadcasts in SR Serbia since 25 May 1979, when news programs such as Dnevnik fully switched to color.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_introduction_of_color_television_in_countries_and_territories#cite_note-112) Color broadcasts had been available from Italy since 1972. |  
| Sierra Leone * | 1978 | SLBS | PAL | [[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_introduction_of_color_television_in_countries_and_territories#cite_note-113) |  

# Timeline of the introduction of color television in countries and territories
## List in alphabetical order by country and territory
| Singapore * | 1974/1975/1977 | Radio Television Singapore (RTS) | PAL | Test transmissions began on 2 May 1974 with imported series such as _The Mary Tyler Moore Show_[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_introduction_of_color_television_in_countries_and_territories#cite_note-114) and was officially introduced on 8 July for the 1974 World Cup Final.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_introduction_of_color_television_in_countries_and_territories#cite_note-colourtvpower-115) The first local programme in colour was the 1974 National Day Parade.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_introduction_of_color_television_in_countries_and_territories#cite_note-116) Newsreels and other programmes were converted on 11 November 1974.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_introduction_of_color_television_in_countries_and_territories#cite_note-Nov11-117) Full-time color broadcasts began on 1 November 1975 when the new studio opened; the news operation was converted at the same time.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_introduction_of_color_television_in_countries_and_territories#cite_note-Nov11-117) |  
| Slovakia *. - Slovak Socialist Republic. | 1970/1973/1980 | ČST | SECAM, PAL | First color transmission in 1970 during World Ski Championship which was broadcast in PAL. Adopted SECAM in 1973 with full-color transition in 1980.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_introduction_of_color_television_in_countries_and_territories#cite_note-118) Switched to PAL from 1993. |

### All-mechanical color
Starting before CBS color even got on the air, the U.S. television industry, represented by the National Television System Committee, worked in 1950–1953 to develop a color system that was compatible with existing black-and-white sets and would pass FCC quality standards, with RCA developing the hardware elements. RCA first made publicly announced field tests of the dot sequential color system over its New York station WNBT in July 1951.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-48) When CBS testified before Congress in March 1953 that it had no further plans for its own color system,[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-49) the National Production Authority dropped its ban on the manufacture of color television receivers,[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-50) and the path was open for the NTSC to submit its petition for FCC approval in July 1953, which was granted on 17 December.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-51) The first publicly announced network demonstration of a program using the NTSC "compatible color" system was an episode of NBC's _Kukla, Fran and Ollie_ on 30 August 1953, although it was viewable in color only at the network's headquarters. The first network broadcast to go out over the air in NTSC color was a performance of the opera _Carmen_ on 31 October 1953.

### All-mechanical color
Colour broadcasts from the United States were available to Canadian population centres near the border from the mid-1950s.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-CBC_goes_colour-52) At the time that NTSC colour broadcasting was officially introduced into Canada in 1966, less than one percent of Canadian households had a colour television set.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-CBC_goes_colour-52) Colour television in Canada was launched on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's (CBC) English language TV service on 1 September 1966.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-CBC_goes_colour-52) Private television broadcaster CTV also started colour broadcasts in early September 1966.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-Color_is_Expensive-53) The CBC's French-language service, Radio-Canada, was broadcasting colour programming on its television network for 15 hours a week in 1968.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-54) Full-time colour transmissions started in 1974 on the CBC, with other private sector broadcasters in the country doing so by the end of the 1970s.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-CBC_goes_colour-52)
The following provinces and areas of Canada introduced colour television by the years as stated
*   Saskatchewan, Alberta, Manitoba, British Columbia, Ontario, Quebec (1966; Major networks only – private sector around 1968 to 1972)  
*   Newfoundland and Labrador (1967)  
*   Nova Scotia, New Brunswick (1968)  
*   Prince Edward Island (1969)  
*   Yukon (1971)  
*   Northwest Territories (including Nunavut) (1972; Major networks in large centers, many remote areas in the far north did not get colour until at least 1977 and 1978)

### All-mechanical color
Cuba in 1958 became the second country in the world to introduce color television broadcasting, with Havana's Telecolor Channel 12 and Television Nacional channel 4 using the American NTSC standard and technology patented by RCA. But the color transmissions ended when broadcasting stations were seized in 1960, and did not return until 1975, using equipment acquired from Japan's NEC Corporation, and SECAM equipment from the Soviet Union, adapted for the American NTSC standard.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-55)
Guillermo González Camarena independently invented and developed a field-sequential tricolor disk system in Mexico in the late 1930s, for which he requested a patent in Mexico on 19 August 1940, and in the United States in 1941.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-US2296019-56) González Camarena produced his color television system in his Gon-Cam laboratory for the Mexican market and exported it to the Columbia College of Chicago, which regarded it as the best system in the world.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-Newcomb-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-Gon-Cam1-58) Goldmark had actually applied for a patent for the same field-sequential tricolor system in the US on 7 September 1940,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-Goldmark1-17) while González Camarena had made his Mexican filing 19 days before, on 19 August.

### All-mechanical color
On 31 August 1946, González Camarena sent his first color transmission from his lab in the offices of the Mexican League of Radio Experiments at Lucerna St. No. 1, in Mexico City. The video signal was transmitted at a frequency of 115 MHz and the audio in the 40-metre band. He obtained authorization to make the first publicly announced color broadcast in Mexico, on 8 February 1964, of the program _Paraíso Infantil_ on Mexico City's XHGC-TV, using the NTSC system that had by now been adopted as the standard for color programming.
González Camarena also invented the "simplified Mexican color TV system" as a much simpler and cheaper alternative to the NTSC system.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-Simplified-Mexican-59) Due to its simplicity, NASA used a modified version of the system in its Voyager mission of 1979, to take pictures and video of Jupiter.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-60)
RCA CT-100 at the SPARK Museum of Electrical Invention playing _Superman_. The RCA CT-100 was the first mass-produced color TV set.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-lancasteronline-61)

### All-mechanical color
Starting before CBS color even got on the air, the U.S. television industry, represented by the National Television System Committee, worked in 1950–1953 to develop a color system that was compatible with existing black-and-white sets and would pass FCC quality standards, with RCA developing the hardware elements. RCA first made publicly announced field tests of the dot sequential color system over its New York station WNBT in July 1951.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-48) When CBS testified before Congress in March 1953 that it had no further plans for its own color system,[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-49) the National Production Authority dropped its ban on the manufacture of color television receivers,[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-50) and the path was open for the NTSC to submit its petition for FCC approval in July 1953, which was granted on 17 December.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-51) The first publicly announced network demonstration of a program using the NTSC "compatible color" system was an episode of NBC's _Kukla, Fran and Ollie_ on 30 August 1953, although it was viewable in color only at the network's headquarters. The first network broadcast to go out over the air in NTSC color was a performance of the opera _Carmen_ on 31 October 1953.

### All-mechanical color
Colour broadcasts from the United States were available to Canadian population centres near the border from the mid-1950s.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-CBC_goes_colour-52) At the time that NTSC colour broadcasting was officially introduced into Canada in 1966, less than one percent of Canadian households had a colour television set.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-CBC_goes_colour-52) Colour television in Canada was launched on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's (CBC) English language TV service on 1 September 1966.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-CBC_goes_colour-52) Private television broadcaster CTV also started colour broadcasts in early September 1966.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-Color_is_Expensive-53) The CBC's French-language service, Radio-Canada, was broadcasting colour programming on its television network for 15 hours a week in 1968.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-54) Full-time colour transmissions started in 1974 on the CBC, with other private sector broadcasters in the country doing so by the end of the 1970s.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-CBC_goes_colour-52)
The following provinces and areas of Canada introduced colour television by the years as stated
*   Saskatchewan, Alberta, Manitoba, British Columbia, Ontario, Quebec (1966; Major networks only – private sector around 1968 to 1972)  
*   Newfoundland and Labrador (1967)  
*   Nova Scotia, New Brunswick (1968)  
*   Prince Edward Island (1969)  
*   Yukon (1971)  
*   Northwest Territories (including Nunavut) (1972; Major networks in large centers, many remote areas in the far north did not get colour until at least 1977 and 1978)

### All-mechanical color
Cuba in 1958 became the second country in the world to introduce color television broadcasting, with Havana's Telecolor Channel 12 and Television Nacional channel 4 using the American NTSC standard and technology patented by RCA. But the color transmissions ended when broadcasting stations were seized in 1960, and did not return until 1975, using equipment acquired from Japan's NEC Corporation, and SECAM equipment from the Soviet Union, adapted for the American NTSC standard.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-55)
Guillermo González Camarena independently invented and developed a field-sequential tricolor disk system in Mexico in the late 1930s, for which he requested a patent in Mexico on 19 August 1940, and in the United States in 1941.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-US2296019-56) González Camarena produced his color television system in his Gon-Cam laboratory for the Mexican market and exported it to the Columbia College of Chicago, which regarded it as the best system in the world.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-Newcomb-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-Gon-Cam1-58) Goldmark had actually applied for a patent for the same field-sequential tricolor system in the US on 7 September 1940,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-Goldmark1-17) while González Camarena had made his Mexican filing 19 days before, on 19 August.

### All-mechanical color
On 31 August 1946, González Camarena sent his first color transmission from his lab in the offices of the Mexican League of Radio Experiments at Lucerna St. No. 1, in Mexico City. The video signal was transmitted at a frequency of 115 MHz and the audio in the 40-metre band. He obtained authorization to make the first publicly announced color broadcast in Mexico, on 8 February 1964, of the program _Paraíso Infantil_ on Mexico City's XHGC-TV, using the NTSC system that had by now been adopted as the standard for color programming.
González Camarena also invented the "simplified Mexican color TV system" as a much simpler and cheaper alternative to the NTSC system.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-Simplified-Mexican-59) Due to its simplicity, NASA used a modified version of the system in its Voyager mission of 1979, to take pictures and video of Jupiter.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-60)
RCA CT-100 at the SPARK Museum of Electrical Invention playing _Superman_. The RCA CT-100 was the first mass-produced color TV set.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television#cite_note-lancasteronline-61)

**Neville Gruzman**, AM (14 November 1925—1 May 2005) was an Australian architect, mayor of Woollahra, writer and architectural activist. He is considered to have exerted a decisive influence on Sydney's architecture, mostly through his dedication to designing architecture that reacts to the landscape and to the needs of the client.
Gruzman was born in Sydney, Australia. His parents—Sam Gruzman and Rosalind Gunzburg—were of Russian origin. He was the middle son, with Laurence, the eldest and Des, the youngest. His childhood near Cooper Park, Bellevue Hill, exerted a certain influence on him regarding his attitude towards landscape. He initially intended to fulfill his mother's wish to study medicine but enrolled for architecture after graduating from Sydney Boys High School.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goad-1) His brother Laurence studied Law and became a barrister and later Queen's Counsel in 1966.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-2)

In the late 1940s Neville entered the University of Sydney, where Beaux Arts was a main subject. The first three years of his studyings were difficult for him as he wasn't good in drawing. However, he profited from his work experiences. He developed an interest in ballrooms, particularly mirrors and reflections, and won some skills with glamorous decoration from an interior decorator, Margaret Jaye. In his fourth year at university, he was attracted to the European Modernists, who influenced and furthered him. Before he graduated, he designed the _Lapin House_, Rose Bay for his aunt. He graduated from the School of Architecture in 1952 and traveled to Europe with other graduates. Returning to Australia, he opened an office with Bill and Ruth Lucas. He read the work _Architectural Beauty in Japan_. He later travelled to Japan on a four-and-a-half month study visit — a journey that would be followed by numerous others to the country.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-mccartney-3) Later, Gruzman was amazed by the work of Frank Lloyd Wright. His understanding of the aspects of planning and of the necessities of an ongoing development grew decisively, in this period. His interests in creative arts extended to craft and in 1964 he founded the Craft Association, Australia's first such entity, later renamed the Crafts Council of NSW[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-4) and then Object: Australian Design Centre.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-5) In about 1967, he devoted himself to teaching; he is reported to have reassured his students attended the classes, regularly, and to have renounced holidays to provide extra tutorials for his students.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goadobituary-6) He also participated in politics, to improve the quality of built environment.
Gruzman had poor health. He suffered from asthma and heart attacks but managed to recover. He also had an accident that led to brain surgery causing the loss of most of his memory, including for details such as door dimensions, which he most attentively relearned.

Gruzman mostly built residential houses in Sydney. His works are varied forms of Modernism known as Organic Modernism, or Regionalism; some show a strong influence by the works of Frank Lloyd Wright. The impressions exerted on him on his trips to Japan—mainly by the traditional post and beam architecture he saw at places like Katsura Imperial Villa—influenced some of the homes he created and into which he eventually included Japanese elements[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-7) (_Goodman House_, Middle Cove). In the 1960s Gruzman gained recognition for private homes built for wealthy and sometimes eccentric clients along Sydney's north shore, such as the _Hill's House_ (1966), designed for a nudist[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-8) and the "theatrical" _Holland House_ (1962),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-9) built for an actress, who would both delight and scare her guests by dancing on the house's handrail-less balcony hanging over a cliff face. His work has been described as "major gestures, very Hollywood glamour."
Gruzman's architectural principles included maximum exposure to sunlight and privacy visually and audibly.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-10)
Gruzman is loosely connected to the Sydney School of architects of the 1950s and 1960s[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-11)—a movement that started in opposition to the International Style of modernism supported by other Australian architects and that has recently been re-discovered by home buyers and architectural fans, leading to a trend to preserve the homes from the period.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-12) However, Gruzman's work deviates from the Sydney School style in important traits; Gruzman himself denied a connection to the movement.
**Montrose Apartments** — Neutral Bay, New South Wales (1954–1955)

Located at 445 Alfred Street, Neutral Bay, this lightweight glass and steel block of eight double-storey apartments was designed by Gruzman in his first year of practice. The building was highly innovative in its planning and visual impact in the landscape. It is a very early example of modernist residential curtain wall construction in Australia.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-13)
Montrose Apartments (1954–55), Neutral Bay in March 2018
**Hills House** — Turramurra, New South Wales (1966, 1983)
Original client was Sam Rosenburg, a nudist and vegetarian. Gruzman's idea was to build a series of hills that surround the site on three sides making it visually and acoustically private. Later, expansion was added for new clients, a family with three children.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goad-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-mccartney-3) The building is referred to by Philip Goad as a product of two iconic 20th-century houses (Wright's Fallingwater and Mies van der Rohe'sFarnsworth House) that created the ultimate diagram of abstract shelter in the landscape.

**Neville Gruzman**, AM (14 November 1925—1 May 2005) was an Australian architect, mayor of Woollahra, writer and architectural activist. He is considered to have exerted a decisive influence on Sydney's architecture, mostly through his dedication to designing architecture that reacts to the landscape and to the needs of the client.
Gruzman was born in Sydney, Australia. His parents—Sam Gruzman and Rosalind Gunzburg—were of Russian origin. He was the middle son, with Laurence, the eldest and Des, the youngest. His childhood near Cooper Park, Bellevue Hill, exerted a certain influence on him regarding his attitude towards landscape. He initially intended to fulfill his mother's wish to study medicine but enrolled for architecture after graduating from Sydney Boys High School.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goad-1) His brother Laurence studied Law and became a barrister and later Queen's Counsel in 1966.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-2)
texts.1:
In the late 1940s Neville entered the University of Sydney, where Beaux Arts was a main subject. The first three years of his studyings were difficult for him as he wasn't good in drawing. However, he profited from his work experiences. He developed an interest in ballrooms, particularly mirrors and reflections, and won some skills with glamorous decoration from an interior decorator, Margaret Jaye. In his fourth year at university, he was attracted to the European Modernists, who influenced and furthered him. Before he graduated, he designed the _Lapin House_, Rose Bay for his aunt. He graduated from the School of Architecture in 1952 and traveled to Europe with other graduates. Returning to Australia, he opened an office with Bill and Ruth Lucas. He read the work _Architectural Beauty in Japan_. He later travelled to Japan on a four-and-a-half month study visit — a journey that would be followed by numerous others to the country.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-mccartney-3) Later, Gruzman was amazed by the work of Frank Lloyd Wright. His understanding of the aspects of planning and of the necessities of an ongoing development grew decisively, in this period. His interests in creative arts extended to craft and in 1964 he founded the Craft Association, Australia's first such entity, later renamed the Crafts Council of NSW[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-4) and then Object: Australian Design Centre.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-5) In about 1967, he devoted himself to teaching; he is reported to have reassured his students attended the classes, regularly, and to have renounced holidays to provide extra tutorials for his students.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goadobituary-6) He also participated in politics, to improve the quality of built environment.
Gruzman had poor health. He suffered from asthma and heart attacks but managed to recover. He also had an accident that led to brain surgery causing the loss of most of his memory, including for details such as door dimensions, which he most attentively relearned.
texts.2:
Gruzman mostly built residential houses in Sydney. His works are varied forms of Modernism known as Organic Modernism, or Regionalism; some show a strong influence by the works of Frank Lloyd Wright. The impressions exerted on him on his trips to Japan—mainly by the traditional post and beam architecture he saw at places like Katsura Imperial Villa—influenced some of the homes he created and into which he eventually included Japanese elements[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-7) (_Goodman House_, Middle Cove). In the 1960s Gruzman gained recognition for private homes built for wealthy and sometimes eccentric clients along Sydney's north shore, such as the _Hill's House_ (1966), designed for a nudist[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-8) and the "theatrical" _Holland House_ (1962),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-9) built for an actress, who would both delight and scare her guests by dancing on the house's handrail-less balcony hanging over a cliff face. His work has been described as "major gestures, very Hollywood glamour."
Gruzman's architectural principles included maximum exposure to sunlight and privacy visually and audibly.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-10)
Gruzman is loosely connected to the Sydney School of architects of the 1950s and 1960s[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-11)—a movement that started in opposition to the International Style of modernism supported by other Australian architects and that has recently been re-discovered by home buyers and architectural fans, leading to a trend to preserve the homes from the period.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-12) However, Gruzman's work deviates from the Sydney School style in important traits; Gruzman himself denied a connection to the movement.

texts.3:

The building was highly innovative in its planning and visual impact in the landscape. It is a very early example of modernist residential curtain wall construction in Australia.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-13)
Montrose Apartments (1954–55), Neutral Bay in March 2018

A prominent African American architect, he was the first Black student to be admitted to and graduate from the University of Pennsylvania’s Department of Architecture.

**Neville Gruzman**, AM (14 November 1925—1 May 2005) was an Australian architect, mayor of Woollahra, writer and architectural activist. He is considered to have exerted a decisive influence on Sydney's architecture, mostly through his dedication to designing architecture that reacts to the landscape and to the needs of the client.
Gruzman was born in Sydney, Australia. His parents—Sam Gruzman and Rosalind Gunzburg—were of Russian origin. He was the middle son, with Laurence, the eldest and Des, the youngest. His childhood near Cooper Park, Bellevue Hill, exerted a certain influence on him regarding his attitude towards landscape. He initially intended to fulfill his mother's wish to study medicine but enrolled for architecture after graduating from Sydney Boys High School.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goad-1) His brother Laurence studied Law and became a barrister and later Queen's Counsel in 1966.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-2)

In the late 1940s Neville entered the University of Sydney, where Beaux Arts was a main subject. The first three years of his studyings were difficult for him as he wasn't good in drawing. However, he profited from his work experiences. He developed an interest in ballrooms, particularly mirrors and reflections, and won some skills with glamorous decoration from an interior decorator, Margaret Jaye. In his fourth year at university, he was attracted to the European Modernists, who influenced and furthered him. Before he graduated, he designed the _Lapin House_, Rose Bay for his aunt. He graduated from the School of Architecture in 1952 and traveled to Europe with other graduates. Returning to Australia, he opened an office with Bill and Ruth Lucas. He read the work _Architectural Beauty in Japan_. He later travelled to Japan on a four-and-a-half month study visit — a journey that would be followed by numerous others to the country.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-mccartney-3) Later, Gruzman was amazed by the work of Frank Lloyd Wright. His understanding of the aspects of planning and of the necessities of an ongoing development grew decisively, in this period. His interests in creative arts extended to craft and in 1964 he founded the Craft Association, Australia's first such entity, later renamed the Crafts Council of NSW[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-4) and then Object: Australian Design Centre.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-5) In about 1967, he devoted himself to teaching; he is reported to have reassured his students attended the classes, regularly, and to have renounced holidays to provide extra tutorials for his students.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goadobituary-6) He also participated in politics, to improve the quality of built environment.
Gruzman had poor health. He suffered from asthma and heart attacks but managed to recover. He also had an accident that led to brain surgery causing the loss of most of his memory, including for details such as door dimensions, which he most attentively relearned.

Gruzman mostly built residential houses in Sydney. His works are varied forms of Modernism known as Organic Modernism, or Regionalism; some show a strong influence by the works of Frank Lloyd Wright. The impressions exerted on him on his trips to Japan—mainly by the traditional post and beam architecture he saw at places like Katsura Imperial Villa—influenced some of the homes he created and into which he eventually included Japanese elements[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-7) (_Goodman House_, Middle Cove). In the 1960s Gruzman gained recognition for private homes built for wealthy and sometimes eccentric clients along Sydney's north shore, such as the _Hill's House_ (1966), designed for a nudist[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-8) and the "theatrical" _Holland House_ (1962),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-9) built for an actress, who would both delight and scare her guests by dancing on the house's handrail-less balcony hanging over a cliff face. His work has been described as "major gestures, very Hollywood glamour."
Gruzman's architectural principles included maximum exposure to sunlight and privacy visually and audibly.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-10)
Gruzman is loosely connected to the Sydney School of architects of the 1950s and 1960s[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-11)—a movement that started in opposition to the International Style of modernism supported by other Australian architects and that has recently been re-discovered by home buyers and architectural fans, leading to a trend to preserve the homes from the period.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-12) However, Gruzman's work deviates from the Sydney School style in important traits; Gruzman himself denied a connection to the movement.
**Montrose Apartments** — Neutral Bay, New South Wales (1954–1955)

Located at 445 Alfred Street, Neutral Bay, this lightweight glass and steel block of eight double-storey apartments was designed by Gruzman in his first year of practice. The building was highly innovative in its planning and visual impact in the landscape. It is a very early example of modernist residential curtain wall construction in Australia.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-13)
Montrose Apartments (1954–55), Neutral Bay in March 2018
**Hills House** — Turramurra, New South Wales (1966, 1983)
Original client was Sam Rosenburg, a nudist and vegetarian. Gruzman's idea was to build a series of hills that surround the site on three sides making it visually and acoustically private. Later, expansion was added for new clients, a family with three children.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goad-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-mccartney-3) The building is referred to by Philip Goad as a product of two iconic 20th-century houses (Wright's Fallingwater and Mies van der Rohe'sFarnsworth House) that created the ultimate diagram of abstract shelter in the landscape.

In the end, there were too many conditions, among them that Gruzman's grandchildren should be allowed to live in the house and that an adjoining property, also owned by the family, should be an architecture centre or gallery.
"And that was just the start of it," says the trust director, Peter Watts. There was no money to maintain the house and there were problems of access. Watts was also concerned with establishing the architectural significance of the 1958 house, which had been extended in 1963 and again in the early 1990s.
There was another big problem. Gruzman's wife, Margot, and her two children were not so enthused by the idea. As Watts put it: "We had some concerns about the views of other members of the family."
The property is in Gruzman's name, and only his executors know for sure what he intended for the house. Built on a cliff-like site, it is known primarily for its beautiful living room, once described by Joern Utzon as the best in Australia.
Here, his architecture students from the University of NSW would be taken by Gruzman "to reflect", says Professor Graham Bell, program head of architecture.
The house is nestled in gum trees and seems to float high above the eye level of passers-by. Its design is influenced by the work of Frank Lloyd Wright and provincial Japanese architecture, but as Gruzman once said, none of his buildings can be readily identified. Unlike Harry Seidler's work, which, Gruzman once wrote, demonstrated "an insensitivity to human need", Gruzman's signature was not obvious.
He made his name designing homes, mainly on Sydney's North Shore, in the 1950s and '60s. Watts believes his houses were "one-off major gestures, very Hollywood glamour".
Elf-like, with high cheekbones and a long, thin face, like his brother, the late Laurence Gruzman, QC, Neville Gruzman appeared to see himself in the third person. _Gruzman on Gruzman_ was the title he gave to a lecture he once delivered to the Australian Institute of Architects.

He told his audience: "I really dislike Gruzman because he is the most aggravating, demanding, sometimes impossible person I have ever known - nothing is ever done well enough to satisfy him - he is concerned for reaching for the stars … the result is that he's given me two heart attacks, caused me to have a quadruple bypass and in the end will be the death of me … Gruzman was born in 1928."
In fact, Gruzman was born in 1925, as was noted on the order of service leaflet given to mourners yesterday at St Mark's Anglican Church, Darling Point.
He continued his lecture: "Gruzman grew up in the Depression - as a result he has a depression mentality - he will never throw anything away … His father died in 1931 as the result of the stress of the Depression, during which he lost his health and most of his wealth. Gruzman's widowed mother set out to bring up her three sons on a tiny income, ensuring they got love, affection and a good education."
His father, Samuel Gruzman, had a pub in Matraville, and it is understood he and his wife, Rosalind, had migrated to Australia and were Jewish. However, Laurence and Neville Gruzman subsequently became members of the Church of England.
Laurence was admitted to the selective Sydney Boys High School, so his sibling, Neville, went there too.
At the University of Sydney, one of Neville's tutors was the _Herald_ cartoonist and architect George Molnar, who was, Gruzman said in his lecture, a mentor and friend who "helped to set him on course for the rest of his life".
Graduating in 1952, Gruzman soon began the first of his many journeys to Europe, Japan and South-East Asia. He was 39 when he married Margot Lovell, who had been married before to a member of the Ryrie family, known for their grazing interests. She had a son, Tasker, and daughter, Prudence, who later married Tony Keulemans, a former ABC broadcaster and academic.

Keulemans was one of many Sydney-siders Gruzman sued. For some time in the 1970s, Keulemans and his wife lived in an apartment in New South Head Road, Edgecliff, one of many properties Gruzman had acquired near his main home.
Initiating the legal action, Gruzman said the apartment was not a gift but had been lent to Keulemans and he wanted it back. The case was to have been heard in August.
Acting for Keulemans is Jeffrey Hilton, SC, who for many years had been the focal point for many disgruntled former Gruzman clients. Hilton, a family friend of Gruzman's, had fallen out with the architect over some bills Gruzman presented to Hilton for proposed changes to the attic in his home.
Hilton complained to Gruzman about the bills, which totalled nearly $30,000. Gruzman wrote back: "Dear Jeff, many years ago I decided that I wouldn't work for Jewish clients …"
The letter, written in 1992, was released to the press by Hilton in 1996. Uproar. At the time, Gruzman was mayor of Woollahra, whose boundaries take in so many suburbs that are home to powerful Jewish networks.
Gruzman did not bow to pressure from the council and even the Premier, Bob Carr, to resign. He apologised, but denied being a racist, although Gruzman said he had suffered from "aggravation" in dealing with Jews, who had "different ways of practising" business.
He stepped down later in 1996, saying his year as mayor had been "interesting" with "some downsides".
Gruzman was considering writing a book, which, he said, "may be called _The Jeffrey Hilton Affair_, or something like that".
Until that affair, Gruzman's many legal battles were not aired publicly, but as the journalist David Marr wrote in 1998, the architect had been involved in litigation almost as long as he had been practising architecture. Court records showed about 30 Gruzman cases going back to the late 1950s, from which he seemed to have won more than $1 million. Like Laurence, Gruzman gravitated towards a fight.

And he did not flatter. In the _Herald_, he once wrote that "most architects have lost the plot as to their role in creating harmonious, serene built environments and their need to build well-detailed, good buildings".
He was three times reported to the Royal Australian Institute of Architects for criticising the work of others, including Seidler's. On each occasion, Gruzman told his audience at the _Gruzman on Gruzman_ lecture, he was "quite rightly, exonerated".
He was not only litigious, but accident prone. He won damages for injuries he received in accidents, including a crash between an army van and his Rolls Royce Corniche in Darlingurst.
In 1981, he needed three months to recover from a virus he caught in Sri Lanka. Then, when he returned to work, he hit his head on scaffolding. The result was a subdural hematoma and three brain operations. That was followed by two heart attacks and the bypass.
At the funeral service yesterday, Tasker Ryrie said Gruzman had been admitted to St Vincent's Hospital nearly 40 times in 30 years. He died there, at St Vincent's Sacred Heart Hospice, on May Day.
All his fights were over, his passions spent. In the words of Ecclesiastes, read yesterday by his grandson, James Keulemans, in his life, as in all others, there was "a time to love, a time to hate, a time of war, and a time of peace".

**Harry Seidler** (25 June 1923–9 March 2006) was an Austrian-born Australian architect who is considered to be one of the leading exponents of Modernism's methodology in Australia and the first architect to fully express the principles of the Bauhaus in Australia.
Seidler designed about 119 buildings (96 of which were in his home state of New South Wales) but some have since been demolished or altered in a non-Seidler manner, and he received much recognition for his contribution to the architecture of Australia. Seidler consistently won architectural awards every decade throughout his Australian career of almost 58 years across the varied categories – his residential work from 1950, his commercial work from 1964, and his public commissions from the 1970s. He was a controversial figure throughout his long career as he regularly publicly criticised planning authorities and the planning system in Sydney.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-1)

Seidler was born in Vienna, Austria, the son of a Jewish clothing manufacturer. Soon after Nazi Germany annexed Austria in 1938, his older brother Marcell, who was already in England, obtained a visa for Harry to join him as a student in Cambridge.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-NSW_Library_Internment-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-3)

## Architecture education
[edit]
Harry Seidler (right) with Walter Gropius in Sydney 1954
In England, he studied building and construction at Cambridgeshire Technical School. Even though he was categorised by British wartime tribunal as a "Category C – no risk" refugee fleeing the Nazis,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-4) because he was born in Austria, on 12 May 1940, he was interned by the British authorities as an enemy alien,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-5) where he was in internment camps first at Huyton near Liverpool, then on the Isle of Man before being shipped to Quebec, Canada and continued to be interned[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-6) until October 1941, when he was released on probational release from internment to study architecture at the University of Manitoba in Winnipeg, where he graduated with first class honours in 1944.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-arch-7)
After working briefly for an architectural firm in Toronto, Seidler (at the age of 21) became a registered architect in Ontario, in February 1945.
Although he was ten years old when the Bauhaus was closed, Seidler's analysts invariably associate him with the Bauhaus because he later studied under emigrant Bauhaus teachers in the USA. He attended Harvard Graduate School of Design under Walter Gropius and Marcel Breuer on a scholarship in 1945/46,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-innmod-8) and during the university winter (Christmas) inter-semester approximate four weeks break Seidler worked with Alvar Aalto in Boston drawing up plans for the Baker dormitory at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. He then studied visual aesthetics at Black Mountain College under the painter Josef Albers in mid 1946 for the US summer.

## Early career outside Australia
[edit]
Seidler worked as the first ever assistant to modernist architect Marcel Breuer in New York from late 1946 until March 1948.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-arch-7) Seidler also worked in Rio de Janeiro with the architect Oscar Niemeyer for almost two months from shortly after 20 April to early June 1948.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-9)
Rose Seidler House, Wahroonga
Australia Square
Seidler's parents migrated to Sydney, Australia in 1946, and (while he was working for Breuer in New York) in late 1947 or early 1948, his mother wrote to him to commission him to come to Sydney to design their home. Seidler arrived in Sydney on (likely) 20 June 1948 (which was a few days before his 25th birthday), with no intention to remain in Australia, but to stay only until the house was finished.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-10) The house became known as the Rose Seidler House in Wahroonga, in remote bushland of a suburb on Sydney's Upper North Shore. This project was the first completely modern domestic residence to fully express the philosophy and visual language of the Bauhaus in Australia and won the Sulman Award of 1951. From the huge publicity of this house, others approached Seidler to design their homes. With so many clients and his enjoyment of the Sydney climate and harbour views, Seidler decided to stay in Australia.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-11) The Rose Seidler House became a house-museum in 1991.
In 1952, Seidler successfully appealed against Ku-ring-gai Council's refusal to approve his design of a glass house in Roseville.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-13)

In the end, there were too many conditions, among them that Gruzman's grandchildren should be allowed to live in the house and that an adjoining property, also owned by the family, should be an architecture centre or gallery.
"And that was just the start of it," says the trust director, Peter Watts. There was no money to maintain the house and there were problems of access. Watts was also concerned with establishing the architectural significance of the 1958 house, which had been extended in 1963 and again in the early 1990s.
There was another big problem. Gruzman's wife, Margot, and her two children were not so enthused by the idea. As Watts put it: "We had some concerns about the views of other members of the family."
The property is in Gruzman's name, and only his executors know for sure what he intended for the house. Built on a cliff-like site, it is known primarily for its beautiful living room, once described by Joern Utzon as the best in Australia.
Here, his architecture students from the University of NSW would be taken by Gruzman "to reflect", says Professor Graham Bell, program head of architecture.
The house is nestled in gum trees and seems to float high above the eye level of passers-by. Its design is influenced by the work of Frank Lloyd Wright and provincial Japanese architecture, but as Gruzman once said, none of his buildings can be readily identified. Unlike Harry Seidler's work, which, Gruzman once wrote, demonstrated "an insensitivity to human need", Gruzman's signature was not obvious.
He made his name designing homes, mainly on Sydney's North Shore, in the 1950s and '60s. Watts believes his houses were "one-off major gestures, very Hollywood glamour".
Elf-like, with high cheekbones and a long, thin face, like his brother, the late Laurence Gruzman, QC, Neville Gruzman appeared to see himself in the third person. _Gruzman on Gruzman_ was the title he gave to a lecture he once delivered to the Australian Institute of Architects.
texts.1:
He told his audience: "I really dislike Gruzman because he is the most aggravating, demanding, sometimes impossible person I have ever known - nothing is ever done well enough to satisfy him - he is concerned for reaching for the stars … the result is that he's given me two heart attacks, caused me to have a quadruple bypass and in the end will be the death of me … Gruzman was born in 1928."
In fact, Gruzman was born in 1925, as was noted on the order of service leaflet given to mourners yesterday at St Mark's Anglican Church, Darling Point.
He continued his lecture: "Gruzman grew up in the Depression - as a result he has a depression mentality - he will never throw anything away … His father died in 1931 as the result of the stress of the Depression, during which he lost his health and most of his wealth. Gruzman's widowed mother set out to bring up her three sons on a tiny income, ensuring they got love, affection and a good education."
His father, Samuel Gruzman, had a pub in Matraville, and it is understood he and his wife, Rosalind, had migrated to Australia and were Jewish. However, Laurence and Neville Gruzman subsequently became members of the Church of England.
Laurence was admitted to the selective Sydney Boys High School, so his sibling, Neville, went there too.
At the University of Sydney, one of Neville's tutors was the _Herald_ cartoonist and architect George Molnar, who was, Gruzman said in his lecture, a mentor and friend who "helped to set him on course for the rest of his life".
Graduating in 1952, Gruzman soon began the first of his many journeys to Europe, Japan and South-East Asia. He was 39 when he married Margot Lovell, who had been married before to a member of the Ryrie family, known for their grazing interests. She had a son, Tasker, and daughter, Prudence, who later married Tony Keulemans, a former ABC broadcaster and academic.
texts.2:
Keulemans was one of many Sydney-siders Gruzman sued. For some time in the 1970s, Keulemans and his wife lived in an apartment in New South Head Road, Edgecliff, one of many properties Gruzman had acquired near his main home.
Initiating the legal action, Gruzman said the apartment was not a gift but had been lent to Keulemans and he wanted it back. The case was to have been heard in August.
Acting for Keulemans is Jeffrey Hilton, SC, who for many years had been the focal point for many disgruntled former Gruzman clients. Hilton, a family friend of Gruzman's, had fallen out with the architect over some bills Gruzman presented to Hilton for proposed changes to the attic in his home.
Hilton complained to Gruzman about the bills, which totalled nearly $30,000. Gruzman wrote back: "Dear Jeff, many years ago I decided that I wouldn't work for Jewish clients …"
The letter, written in 1992, was released to the press by Hilton in 1996. Uproar. At the time, Gruzman was mayor of Woollahra, whose boundaries take in so many suburbs that are home to powerful Jewish networks.
Gruzman did not bow to pressure from the council and even the Premier, Bob Carr, to resign. He apologised, but denied being a racist, although Gruzman said he had suffered from "aggravation" in dealing with Jews, who had "different ways of practising" business.
He stepped down later in 1996, saying his year as mayor had been "interesting" with "some downsides".
Gruzman was considering writing a book, which, he said, "may be called _The Jeffrey Hilton Affair_, or something like that".
Until that affair, Gruzman's many legal battles were not aired publicly, but as the journalist David Marr wrote in 1998, the architect had been involved in litigation almost as long as he had been practising architecture. Court records showed about 30 Gruzman cases going back to the late 1950s, from which he seemed to have won more than $1 million. Like Laurence, Gruzman gravitated towards a fight.
texts.3:
And he did not flatter. In the _Herald_, he once wrote that "most architects have lost the plot as to their role in creating harmonious, serene built environments and their need to build well-detailed, good buildings".
He was three times reported to the Royal Australian Institute of Architects for criticising the work of others, including Seidler's. On each occasion, Gruzman told his audience at the _Gruzman on Gruzman_ lecture, he was "quite rightly, exonerated".
He was not only litigious, but accident prone. He won damages for injuries he received in accidents, including a crash between an army van and his Rolls Royce Corniche in Darlingurst.
In 1981, he needed three months to recover from a virus he caught in Sri Lanka. Then, when he returned to work, he hit his head on scaffolding. The result was a subdural hematoma and three brain operations. That was followed by two heart attacks and the bypass.
At the funeral service yesterday, Tasker Ryrie said Gruzman had been admitted to St Vincent's Hospital nearly 40 times in 30 years. He died there, at St Vincent's Sacred Heart Hospice, on May Day.
All his fights were over, his passions spent. In the words of Ecclesiastes, read yesterday by his grandson, James Keulemans, in his life, as in all others, there was "a time to love, a time to hate, a time of war, and a time of peace".

**Harry Seidler** (25 June 1923–9 March 2006) was an Austrian-born Australian architect who is considered to be one of the leading exponents of Modernism's methodology in Australia and the first architect to fully express the principles of the Bauhaus in Australia.
Seidler designed about 119 buildings (96 of which were in his home state of New South Wales) but some have since been demolished or altered in a non-Seidler manner, and he received much recognition for his contribution to the architecture of Australia. Seidler consistently won architectural awards every decade throughout his Australian career of almost 58 years across the varied categories – his residential work from 1950, his commercial work from 1964, and his public commissions from the 1970s. He was a controversial figure throughout his long career as he regularly publicly criticised planning authorities and the planning system in Sydney.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-1)
texts.1: Seidler was born in Vienna, Austria, the son of a Jewish clothing manufacturer. Soon after Nazi Germany annexed Austria in 1938, his older brother Marcell, who was already in England, obtained a visa for Harry to join him as a student in Cambridge.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-NSW_Library_Internment-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-3)
texts.2:
## Architecture education
[edit]
Harry Seidler (right) with Walter Gropius in Sydney 1954
In England, he studied building and construction at Cambridgeshire Technical School. Even though he was categorised by British wartime tribunal as a "Category C – no risk" refugee fleeing the Nazis,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-4) because he was born in Austria, on 12 May 1940, he was interned by the British authorities as an enemy alien,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-5) where he was in internment camps first at Huyton near Liverpool, then on the Isle of Man before being shipped to Quebec, Canada and continued to be interned[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-6) until October 1941, when he was released on probational release from internment to study architecture at the University of Manitoba in Winnipeg, where he graduated with first class honours in 1944.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-arch-7)
After working briefly for an architectural firm in Toronto, Seidler (at the age of 21) became a registered architect in Ontario, in February 1945.
Although he was ten years old when the Bauhaus was closed, Seidler's analysts invariably associate him with the Bauhaus because he later studied under emigrant Bauhaus teachers in the USA. He attended Harvard Graduate School of Design under Walter Gropius and Marcel Breuer on a scholarship in 1945/46,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-innmod-8) and during the university winter (Christmas) inter-semester approximate four weeks break Seidler worked with Alvar Aalto in Boston drawing up plans for the Baker dormitory at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. He then studied visual aesthetics at Black Mountain College under the painter Josef Albers in mid 1946 for the US summer.
texts.3:
## Early career outside Australia
[edit]
Seidler worked as the first ever assistant to modernist architect Marcel Breuer in New York from late 1946 until March 1948.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-arch-7) Seidler also worked in Rio de Janeiro with the architect Oscar Niemeyer for almost two months from shortly after 20 April to early June 1948.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-9)
Rose Seidler House, Wahroonga
Australia Square
Seidler's parents migrated to Sydney, Australia in 1946, and (while he was working for Breuer in New York) in late 1947 or early 1948, his mother wrote to him to commission him to come to Sydney to design their home. Seidler arrived in Sydney on (likely) 20 June 1948 (which was a few days before his 25th birthday), with no intention to remain in Australia, but to stay only until the house was finished.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-10) The house became known as the Rose Seidler House in Wahroonga, in remote bushland of a suburb on Sydney's Upper North Shore. This project was the first completely modern domestic residence to fully express the philosophy and visual language of the Bauhaus in Australia and won the Sulman Award of 1951. From the huge publicity of this house, others approached Seidler to design their homes. With so many clients and his enjoyment of the Sydney climate and harbour views, Seidler decided to stay in Australia.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-11) The Rose Seidler House became a house-museum in 1991.
In 1952, Seidler successfully appealed against Ku-ring-gai Council's refusal to approve his design of a glass house in Roseville.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler#cite_note-13)

**Neville Gruzman**, AM (14 November 1925—1 May 2005) was an Australian architect, mayor of Woollahra, writer and architectural activist. He is considered to have exerted a decisive influence on Sydney's architecture, mostly through his dedication to designing architecture that reacts to the landscape and to the needs of the client.
Gruzman was born in Sydney, Australia. His parents—Sam Gruzman and Rosalind Gunzburg—were of Russian origin. He was the middle son, with Laurence, the eldest and Des, the youngest. His childhood near Cooper Park, Bellevue Hill, exerted a certain influence on him regarding his attitude towards landscape. He initially intended to fulfill his mother's wish to study medicine but enrolled for architecture after graduating from Sydney Boys High School.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goad-1) His brother Laurence studied Law and became a barrister and later Queen's Counsel in 1966.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-2)
texts.1:
In the late 1940s Neville entered the University of Sydney, where Beaux Arts was a main subject. The first three years of his studyings were difficult for him as he wasn't good in drawing. However, he profited from his work experiences. He developed an interest in ballrooms, particularly mirrors and reflections, and won some skills with glamorous decoration from an interior decorator, Margaret Jaye. In his fourth year at university, he was attracted to the European Modernists, who influenced and furthered him. Before he graduated, he designed the _Lapin House_, Rose Bay for his aunt. He graduated from the School of Architecture in 1952 and traveled to Europe with other graduates. Returning to Australia, he opened an office with Bill and Ruth Lucas. He read the work _Architectural Beauty in Japan_. He later travelled to Japan on a four-and-a-half month study visit — a journey that would be followed by numerous others to the country.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-mccartney-3) Later, Gruzman was amazed by the work of Frank Lloyd Wright. His understanding of the aspects of planning and of the necessities of an ongoing development grew decisively, in this period. His interests in creative arts extended to craft and in 1964 he founded the Craft Association, Australia's first such entity, later renamed the Crafts Council of NSW[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-4) and then Object: Australian Design Centre.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-5) In about 1967, he devoted himself to teaching; he is reported to have reassured his students attended the classes, regularly, and to have renounced holidays to provide extra tutorials for his students.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goadobituary-6) He also participated in politics, to improve the quality of built environment.
Gruzman had poor health. He suffered from asthma and heart attacks but managed to recover. He also had an accident that led to brain surgery causing the loss of most of his memory, including for details such as door dimensions, which he most attentively relearned.
texts.2:
Gruzman mostly built residential houses in Sydney. His works are varied forms of Modernism known as Organic Modernism, or Regionalism; some show a strong influence by the works of Frank Lloyd Wright. The impressions exerted on him on his trips to Japan—mainly by the traditional post and beam architecture he saw at places like Katsura Imperial Villa—influenced some of the homes he created and into which he eventually included Japanese elements[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-7) (_Goodman House_, Middle Cove). In the 1960s Gruzman gained recognition for private homes built for wealthy and sometimes eccentric clients along Sydney's north shore, such as the _Hill's House_ (1966), designed for a nudist[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-8) and the "theatrical" _Holland House_ (1962),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-9) built for an actress, who would both delight and scare her guests by dancing on the house's handrail-less balcony hanging over a cliff face. His work has been described as "major gestures, very Hollywood glamour."
Gruzman's architectural principles included maximum exposure to sunlight and privacy visually and audibly.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-10)
Gruzman is loosely connected to the Sydney School of architects of the 1950s and 1960s[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-11)—a movement that started in opposition to the International Style of modernism supported by other Australian architects and that has recently been re-discovered by home buyers and architectural fans, leading to a trend to preserve the homes from the period.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-12) However, Gruzman's work deviates from the Sydney School style in important traits; Gruzman himself denied a connection to the movement.
**Montrose Apartments** — Neutral Bay, New South Wales (1954–1955)
texts.3:
Located at 445 Alfred Street, Neutral Bay, this lightweight glass and steel block of eight double-storey apartments was designed by Gruzman in his first year of practice. The building was highly innovative in its planning and visual impact in the landscape. It is a very early example of modernist residential curtain wall construction in Australia.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-13)
Montrose Apartments (1954–55), Neutral Bay in March 2018
**Hills House** — Turramurra, New South Wales (1966, 1983)
Original client was Sam Rosenburg, a nudist and vegetarian. Gruzman's idea was to build a series of hills that surround the site on three sides making it visually and acoustically private. Later, expansion was added for new clients, a family with three children.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goad-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-mccartney-3) The building is referred to by Philip Goad as a product of two iconic 20th-century houses (Wright's Fallingwater and Mies van der Rohe'sFarnsworth House) that created the ultimate diagram of abstract shelter in the landscape.

# Council Flays Australian Mayor Who `would Not Work for Jews’
February 20, 1996 See Original Daily Bulletin From This Date
A Jewish-born mayor of a suburb near here has been censured by his own council after the release of a letter from 1992 in which he said he “wouldn’t work for Jewish clients.”
Mayor Neville Gruzman, who is a member of the Church of England, was booed and heckled at a recent meeting of the Woollahra Council as a result of the letter.
Jeffrey Hilton, a Jewish lawyer in Sydney who received the letter, said Gruzman had originally agreed to work for him because he has a non-Jewish wife, which, in Gruzman’s eyes, makes him a “better” Jew.
The council eventually decided, after a long and bitter debate, to give Gruzman one week “to show cause why he should not resign.”
Gruzman said his comments “were not made for any racist reason” but because he had difficulty in dealing with the “different ways of practicing” business that Jews use. He also said dealing with Jews could result in “aggravation.”
During the debate, the only Jewish member of the council, Julian Leeser, said Gruzman had made another anti-Jewish remark in an interview with a national television journalist.
Some council members defended Gruzman, saying that he was being attacked for political reasons.
The New South Wales Jewish Board of Deputies, which represents the jewish community in the area, has publicly criticized the mayor.
The head of the Orthodox Rabbinical Council of New South Wales, Rabbi Selwyn Franklin, had written to all the council members, arguing that “one who has expressed such views should not be entitled to hold public office in Australia.”
The council represents an area where a number of Jews reside and several synagogues exist.
