In the end, there were too many conditions, among them that Gruzman's grandchildren should be allowed to live in the house and that an adjoining property, also owned by the family, should be an architecture centre or gallery.
"And that was just the start of it," says the trust director, Peter Watts. There was no money to maintain the house and there were problems of access. Watts was also concerned with establishing the architectural significance of the 1958 house, which had been extended in 1963 and again in the early 1990s.
There was another big problem. Gruzman's wife, Margot, and her two children were not so enthused by the idea. As Watts put it: "We had some concerns about the views of other members of the family."
The property is in Gruzman's name, and only his executors know for sure what he intended for the house. Built on a cliff-like site, it is known primarily for its beautiful living room, once described by Joern Utzon as the best in Australia.
Here, his architecture students from the University of NSW would be taken by Gruzman "to reflect", says Professor Graham Bell, program head of architecture.
The house is nestled in gum trees and seems to float high above the eye level of passers-by. Its design is influenced by the work of Frank Lloyd Wright and provincial Japanese architecture, but as Gruzman once said, none of his buildings can be readily identified. Unlike Harry Seidler's work, which, Gruzman once wrote, demonstrated "an insensitivity to human need", Gruzman's signature was not obvious.
He made his name designing homes, mainly on Sydney's North Shore, in the 1950s and '60s. Watts believes his houses were "one-off major gestures, very Hollywood glamour".
Elf-like, with high cheekbones and a long, thin face, like his brother, the late Laurence Gruzman, QC, Neville Gruzman appeared to see himself in the third person. _Gruzman on Gruzman_ was the title he gave to a lecture he once delivered to the Australian Institute of Architects.

He told his audience: "I really dislike Gruzman because he is the most aggravating, demanding, sometimes impossible person I have ever known - nothing is ever done well enough to satisfy him - he is concerned for reaching for the stars … the result is that he's given me two heart attacks, caused me to have a quadruple bypass and in the end will be the death of me … Gruzman was born in 1928."
In fact, Gruzman was born in 1925, as was noted on the order of service leaflet given to mourners yesterday at St Mark's Anglican Church, Darling Point.
He continued his lecture: "Gruzman grew up in the Depression - as a result he has a depression mentality - he will never throw anything away … His father died in 1931 as the result of the stress of the Depression, during which he lost his health and most of his wealth. Gruzman's widowed mother set out to bring up her three sons on a tiny income, ensuring they got love, affection and a good education."
His father, Samuel Gruzman, had a pub in Matraville, and it is understood he and his wife, Rosalind, had migrated to Australia and were Jewish. However, Laurence and Neville Gruzman subsequently became members of the Church of England.
Laurence was admitted to the selective Sydney Boys High School, so his sibling, Neville, went there too.
At the University of Sydney, one of Neville's tutors was the _Herald_ cartoonist and architect George Molnar, who was, Gruzman said in his lecture, a mentor and friend who "helped to set him on course for the rest of his life".
Graduating in 1952, Gruzman soon began the first of his many journeys to Europe, Japan and South-East Asia. He was 39 when he married Margot Lovell, who had been married before to a member of the Ryrie family, known for their grazing interests. She had a son, Tasker, and daughter, Prudence, who later married Tony Keulemans, a former ABC broadcaster and academic.

Keulemans was one of many Sydney-siders Gruzman sued. For some time in the 1970s, Keulemans and his wife lived in an apartment in New South Head Road, Edgecliff, one of many properties Gruzman had acquired near his main home.
Initiating the legal action, Gruzman said the apartment was not a gift but had been lent to Keulemans and he wanted it back. The case was to have been heard in August.
Acting for Keulemans is Jeffrey Hilton, SC, who for many years had been the focal point for many disgruntled former Gruzman clients. Hilton, a family friend of Gruzman's, had fallen out with the architect over some bills Gruzman presented to Hilton for proposed changes to the attic in his home.
Hilton complained to Gruzman about the bills, which totalled nearly $30,000. Gruzman wrote back: "Dear Jeff, many years ago I decided that I wouldn't work for Jewish clients …"
The letter, written in 1992, was released to the press by Hilton in 1996. Uproar. At the time, Gruzman was mayor of Woollahra, whose boundaries take in so many suburbs that are home to powerful Jewish networks.
Gruzman did not bow to pressure from the council and even the Premier, Bob Carr, to resign. He apologised, but denied being a racist, although Gruzman said he had suffered from "aggravation" in dealing with Jews, who had "different ways of practising" business.
He stepped down later in 1996, saying his year as mayor had been "interesting" with "some downsides".
Gruzman was considering writing a book, which, he said, "may be called _The Jeffrey Hilton Affair_, or something like that".
Until that affair, Gruzman's many legal battles were not aired publicly, but as the journalist David Marr wrote in 1998, the architect had been involved in litigation almost as long as he had been practising architecture. Court records showed about 30 Gruzman cases going back to the late 1950s, from which he seemed to have won more than $1 million. Like Laurence, Gruzman gravitated towards a fight.

And he did not flatter. In the _Herald_, he once wrote that "most architects have lost the plot as to their role in creating harmonious, serene built environments and their need to build well-detailed, good buildings".
He was three times reported to the Royal Australian Institute of Architects for criticising the work of others, including Seidler's. On each occasion, Gruzman told his audience at the _Gruzman on Gruzman_ lecture, he was "quite rightly, exonerated".
He was not only litigious, but accident prone. He won damages for injuries he received in accidents, including a crash between an army van and his Rolls Royce Corniche in Darlingurst.
In 1981, he needed three months to recover from a virus he caught in Sri Lanka. Then, when he returned to work, he hit his head on scaffolding. The result was a subdural hematoma and three brain operations. That was followed by two heart attacks and the bypass.
At the funeral service yesterday, Tasker Ryrie said Gruzman had been admitted to St Vincent's Hospital nearly 40 times in 30 years. He died there, at St Vincent's Sacred Heart Hospice, on May Day.
All his fights were over, his passions spent. In the words of Ecclesiastes, read yesterday by his grandson, James Keulemans, in his life, as in all others, there was "a time to love, a time to hate, a time of war, and a time of peace".

In the 1980s Gruzman joined the Anti-Wall Committee formed to protect the Sydney Opera House from nearby urban development. In 1997 he chaired the renamed "Save East Circular Quay Committee" convened by Tony Rodi and Paul Johnson,http://www.bbzine.com/archeplus/Eadline34.html in the ensuing battle to stop the desecration of the Sydney Opera House Precinct.
In the 1990s Gruzman became politically active and was elected first as a councillor and then mayor of Woollahra, on a platform of responsible urban development. He was a very passionate and outspoken critic of urban planning in Sydney, and also Sydney architects, notably Harry Seidler. Both his architectural criticism and time as mayor were controversial.
Gruzman began teaching at the University of New South Wales in the 1960s with a number of contemporary modernist architects such as Bill Lucas and Harry Howard. He became an Adjunct Professor and, as a critic of shortening teaching hours and increasing class size, was known for using Saturdays and public holidays to give extra classes to his students at his own home. In 2002 he established two student awards at the Faculty of the Built Environment, both for the best use of urban design in architecture. In his studio practise, beginning from the 1950s, he also employed and trained many notable Sydney architects, including Pritzker Prize winner Glenn Murcutt.

## Portrait and memoirs
In 1970, Gruzman was the subject of the winning entry for the Archibald Prize, painted by Eric Smith. Gruzman sat for Smith several times, and commissioned Smith to contribute mosaics and stained glass for buildings he designed, including the South Head and District Synagogue in Rose Bay, as well as paintings Smith produced for the houses of his clients.
Most of Gruzman's houses were photographed by Max Dupain and David Moore.
Gruzman's memoirs, incorporated into a book written by Philip Goad and featuring many of the Dupain and Moore photographs, was published posthumously in 2006 by Thames & Hudson.
Gruzman was appointed a Member of the Order of Australia (AM) in the 1985 Australia Day Honours.
The _Margot and Neville Gruzman Award for Urban Design in Architecture_ was named after Gruzman due to his commitment in teaching at the University of New South Wales.

Acting for Keulemans is Jeffrey Hilton, SC, who for many years had been the focal point for many disgruntled former Gruzman clients. Hilton, a family friend of Gruzman's, had fallen out with the architect over some bills Gruzman presented to Hilton for proposed changes to the attic in his home.
Hilton complained to Gruzman about the bills, which totalled nearly $30,000. Gruzman wrote back: "Dear Jeff, many years ago I decided that I wouldn't work for Jewish clients …"
The letter, written in 1992, was released to the press by Hilton in 1996. Uproar. At the time, Gruzman was mayor of Woollahra, whose boundaries take in so many suburbs that are home to powerful Jewish networks.
Gruzman did not bow to pressure from the council and even the Premier, Bob Carr, to resign. He apologised, but denied being a racist, although Gruzman said he had suffered from "aggravation" in dealing with Jews, who had "different ways of practising" business.
He stepped down later in 1996, saying his year as mayor had been "interesting" with "some downsides".
Gruzman was considering writing a book, which, he said, "may be called _The Jeffrey Hilton Affair_, or something like that".
Until that affair, Gruzman's many legal battles were not aired publicly, but as the journalist David Marr wrote in 1998, the architect had been involved in litigation almost as long as he had been practising architecture. Court records showed about 30 Gruzman cases going back to the late 1950s, from which he seemed to have won more than $1 million. Like Laurence, Gruzman gravitated towards a fight.
texts.3:
And he did not flatter. In the _Herald_, he once wrote that "most architects have lost the plot as to their role in creating harmonious, serene built environments and their need to build well-detailed, good buildings".
He was three times reported to the Royal Australian Institute of Architects for criticising the work of others, including Seidler's. On each occasion, Gruzman told his audience at the _Gruzman on Gruzman_ lecture, he was "quite rightly, exonerated".
He was not only litigious, but accident prone. He won damages for injuries he received in accidents, including a crash between an army van and his Rolls Royce Corniche in Darlingurst.
In 1981, he needed three months to recover from a virus he caught in Sri Lanka. Then, when he returned to work, he hit his head on scaffolding. The result was a subdural hematoma and three brain operations. That was followed by two heart attacks and the bypass.
At the funeral service yesterday, Tasker Ryrie said Gruzman had been admitted to St Vincent's Hospital nearly 40 times in 30 years. He died there, at St Vincent's Sacred Heart Hospice, on May Day.
All his fights were over, his passions spent. In the words of Ecclesiastes, read yesterday by his grandson, James Keulemans, in his life, as in all others, there was "a time to love, a time to hate, a time of war, and a time of peace".

# Council Flays Australian Mayor Who `would Not Work for Jews’
February 20, 1996 See Original Daily Bulletin From This Date
A Jewish-born mayor of a suburb near here has been censured by his own council after the release of a letter from 1992 in which he said he “wouldn’t work for Jewish clients.”
Mayor Neville Gruzman, who is a member of the Church of England, was booed and heckled at a recent meeting of the Woollahra Council as a result of the letter.
Jeffrey Hilton, a Jewish lawyer in Sydney who received the letter, said Gruzman had originally agreed to work for him because he has a non-Jewish wife, which, in Gruzman’s eyes, makes him a “better” Jew.
The council eventually decided, after a long and bitter debate, to give Gruzman one week “to show cause why he should not resign.”
Gruzman said his comments “were not made for any racist reason” but because he had difficulty in dealing with the “different ways of practicing” business that Jews use. He also said dealing with Jews could result in “aggravation.”
During the debate, the only Jewish member of the council, Julian Leeser, said Gruzman had made another anti-Jewish remark in an interview with a national television journalist.
Some council members defended Gruzman, saying that he was being attacked for political reasons.
The New South Wales Jewish Board of Deputies, which represents the jewish community in the area, has publicly criticized the mayor.
The head of the Orthodox Rabbinical Council of New South Wales, Rabbi Selwyn Franklin, had written to all the council members, arguing that “one who has expressed such views should not be entitled to hold public office in Australia.”
The council represents an area where a number of Jews reside and several synagogues exist.

In the 1980s Gruzman joined the Anti-Wall Committee formed to protect the Sydney Opera House from nearby urban development. In 1997 he chaired the renamed "Save East Circular Quay Committee" convened by Tony Rodi and Paul Johnson,http://www.bbzine.com/archeplus/Eadline34.html in the ensuing battle to stop the desecration of the Sydney Opera House Precinct.
In the 1990s Gruzman became politically active and was elected first as a councillor and then mayor of Woollahra, on a platform of responsible urban development. He was a very passionate and outspoken critic of urban planning in Sydney, and also Sydney architects, notably Harry Seidler. Both his architectural criticism and time as mayor were controversial.
Gruzman began teaching at the University of New South Wales in the 1960s with a number of contemporary modernist architects such as Bill Lucas and Harry Howard. He became an Adjunct Professor and, as a critic of shortening teaching hours and increasing class size, was known for using Saturdays and public holidays to give extra classes to his students at his own home. In 2002 he established two student awards at the Faculty of the Built Environment, both for the best use of urban design in architecture. In his studio practise, beginning from the 1950s, he also employed and trained many notable Sydney architects, including Pritzker Prize winner Glenn Murcutt.

## Portrait and memoirs
In 1970, Gruzman was the subject of the winning entry for the Archibald Prize, painted by Eric Smith. Gruzman sat for Smith several times, and commissioned Smith to contribute mosaics and stained glass for buildings he designed, including the South Head and District Synagogue in Rose Bay, as well as paintings Smith produced for the houses of his clients.
Most of Gruzman's houses were photographed by Max Dupain and David Moore.
Gruzman's memoirs, incorporated into a book written by Philip Goad and featuring many of the Dupain and Moore photographs, was published posthumously in 2006 by Thames & Hudson.
Gruzman was appointed a Member of the Order of Australia (AM) in the 1985 Australia Day Honours.
The _Margot and Neville Gruzman Award for Urban Design in Architecture_ was named after Gruzman due to his commitment in teaching at the University of New South Wales.
